title: Assistive technology is being reframed as participation infrastructure, but access remains gendered, social, and structurally unequal
source_unit: UN Women and ATscale, Unlocking HER potential: Gender equality through equitable access to assistive technology
geography: Global policy brief drawing on evidence from nearly 50 countries, country consultations, and international literature

observations.period: 2026; assistive technology and gender equality across the life course

denominator.unit: UN Women and ATscale global policy framework

participation_role.value: assistive technology is presented as a prerequisite for women’s meaningful participation in education, employment, family life, leadership, public life, and digital spaces
participation_role.unit: UN Women and ATscale policy framing

rights_route.value: access to assistive technology is treated as an enabler of human rights and gender equality, not a niche or specialized service

access_gap.value: millions of women and girls remain excluded by systems that do not provide gender-responsive, safe, and accessible solutions

life_course.value: the brief uses a life-course perspective to connect assistive technology with autonomy, communication, opportunity, and agency

observations.method: UN Women and ATscale policy brief synthesis connecting assistive technology, disability, gender equality, human rights, and participation across the life course.
observations.uncertainty: The brief is a global policy analysis and evidence synthesis, not a universal prevalence estimate or causal evaluation of assistive-technology provision.
observations.subgroup: Women and girls with disabilities, older women, assistive-technology users, caregivers, workers, students, leaders, and people facing intersecting forms of exclusion.
observations.counterinterpretation: Assistive technology can expand autonomy and participation, but products alone cannot overcome inaccessible institutions, stigma, poverty, violence, or weak service systems.

observations.period: 2026; evidence base for gendered assistive-technology access

denominator.unit: more than 240 survey responses from individuals and organizations across nearly 50 countries

evidence_inputs.value: the brief draws on more than 240 survey responses, country-level consultations, literature review, expert input, and more than 80 sources described in related launch materials

barrier_type.value: barriers are social, economic, and structural as well as technical

intersectionality.value: women and girls with disabilities and those facing intersecting discrimination require explicit attention in system design and provision

policy_endpoint.value: equitable access requires changes in systems rather than treating assistive technology as an individual purchase alone

observations.method: Mixed evidence synthesis using surveys of individuals and organizations, country consultations, literature review, and expert input; the brief organizes the evidence through a systems framework.
observations.uncertainty: The survey and consultation inputs are not a probability sample of all users or countries, and evidence sources may differ in measurement, representation, and quality.
observations.subgroup: Assistive-technology users, women and girls with disabilities, organizations, providers, advocates, policymakers, and communities with different service and financing conditions.
observations.counterinterpretation: A broad evidence base can identify recurring barriers without proving their prevalence or relative importance in every setting.

denominator.unit: People, Products, Provision, Personnel, and Policy dimensions

people.value: systems should center the voices and lived realities of women and girls, especially those with disabilities

products.value: assistive products need to be accessible, safe, appropriate, and responsive to diverse needs

provision.value: financing, service delivery, continuity, and availability shape whether products become usable access

personnel_policy.value: trained personnel and enabling policy are necessary complements to products and user demand

observations.method: Policy brief framework analysis of five interconnected dimensions in assistive-technology systems.
observations.uncertainty: The framework organizes barriers and routes for action but does not assign a universal causal weight or implementation sequence to each dimension.
observations.subgroup: Users, caregivers, service providers, clinicians, educators, employers, designers, procurement authorities, regulators, and funders.
observations.counterinterpretation: A systems framework can prevent product-only thinking, but coordination across five dimensions may increase implementation complexity and resource demands.

observations.period: 2026; policy routes from access to participation and leadership

denominator.unit: UN Women and ATscale recommendation framework

mainstreaming.value: gender-transformative assistive technology should be mainstreamed into national policies and global frameworks

financial_barriers.value: financing and affordability barriers should be reduced, including through subsidies and support for local, women-led production and innovation

workforce_and_design.value: women should participate in product design, governance, and procurement, supported by a gender-balanced workforce and attention to dignity, safety, privacy, and accessibility

service_integration.value: assistive technology should be integrated into health, education, social-protection, and humanitarian systems

observations.method: UN Women and ATscale policy recommendations derived from the 5Ps framework and mixed evidence base.
observations.uncertainty: These recommendations are not a funding audit or implementation evaluation; effectiveness depends on national law, procurement, service capacity, markets, and user-led accountability.
observations.subgroup: Women and girls with disabilities, older people, families, service systems, employers, educators, humanitarian actors, product makers, and public authorities.
observations.counterinterpretation: Integration can improve continuity and reach, but poorly designed mainstreaming can erase disability-specific needs or reproduce gender and household power inequalities.

related_sources.claim: UN Women-hosted PDF of the joint policy brief.
ATscale launch material describing the brief's evidence, structural barriers, and policy actions.
UN Web TV CSW70 launch event describing assistive technology as an enabler of participation, leadership, and decision-making.

boundary: This record adds an assistive-technology route across disability, gender, autonomy, care, education, employment, leadership, digital access, service delivery, and public participation. It uses a global policy brief and mixed evidence synthesis, not a global product-coverage census, raw user-level disability data, representative prevalence estimate, causal impact evaluation, or proof that mainstreaming works without disability-specific provision and user-led accountability.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official ATscale publication page, UN Women-hosted PDF listing, ATscale launch material, and UN Web TV event summary reviewed for the participation framing, evidence base, 5Ps framework, barriers, and policy routes.
